name: Apalai
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_quote: Do ponto de vista fonológico, a palavra é uma seqüência de sílabas em que a penúltima é acentuada: paruru 'banana'. Há um pequeno número de palavras com uma só sílaba. Estas podem receber o acento intensivo dependendo de sua posição em construções maiores

new_statements.quote: Do ponto de vista fonológico, a palavra é uma seqüência de sílabas em que a penúltima é acentuada: parúru "banana". [...] O acento secundário cai em sílabas travadas e em sílabas nasais contíguas a pelo menos uma sílaba não-acentuada: kòⁿxtapanóⁿko "ficando frio", emèʔnóⁿko "romper do dia". O acento secundário pode cair na sílaba inicial das palavras de quatro ou mais sílabas quando a segunda sílaba não é acentuada: xìrikazúru "grama". O padrão acentual tem certa flexibilidade em casos de interação de alguns fatôres acima mencionados. Os padrões acentuais, porém, nunca são contrastivos.
new_statements.translation: From the phonological point of view, the word is a sequence of syllables in which the penultimate is stressed: parúru 'banana'. [...] Secondary stress falls on closed syllables and on nasal syllables adjacent to at least one unstressed syllable: kòⁿxtapanóⁿko 'getting cold', emèʔnóⁿko 'daybreak'. Secondary stress may fall on the initial syllable of words of four or more syllables when the second syllable is unstressed: xìrikazúru 'grass'. The stress pattern has some flexibility in cases where some of the factors mentioned above interact. Stress patterns, however, are never contrastive.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's StressTyp2 penultimate stress (penultimate) and adds: weight/nasality-conditioned secondary stress, an initial secondary stress in 4+ syllable words, phrase-dependent stress of monosyllables, and the statement that stress is never contrastive. This is the published Portuguese form of the phonology of the listed 1964 manuscript (same authors, same translator, same section title), so it stands in for index 0.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary ('intensive') stress on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; stress is never contrastive, so it is not written in the phonemic orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on closed syllables and on nasal syllables adjacent to at least one unstressed syllable; it may also fall on the initial syllable of words of four or more syllables when the second syllable is unstressed (xìrikazúru).
new_statements.exceptions: A small number of monosyllabic words may or may not receive the intensive stress depending on their position in larger constructions (tám 'grandfather'); the pattern shows some flexibility when the factors interact; stress is never contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: Koehn & Koehn's description is of the Apalaí of the lower/central Paru river (village of Camaru), Pará, Brazil, fieldwork 1962-63; they deliberately avoided the Wayana-influenced upper Paru (Koehn & Koehn 1971: 17).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Portuguese sentence and the secondary-stress/non-contrastive sentences are verbatim in the held SIL re-edition ( p. 5) and, after downloading the original 1971 scan from the Curt Nimuendajú library, confirmed at printed p. 26 exactly as the locator says. (2) Deciding source: a 1971 primary phonology article by the language's principal describers (Koehn & Koehn, SIL), not a database paraphrase; StressTyp2/Gordon 2002 are listed only as secondary refs. Best available: the only fuller work is the same authors' 1986 HAL sketch (not yet obtained, paywalled); Derbyshire 1999:28 (held elsewhere in the catalog tree) independently gives Apalai penultimate stress; Gomes & Ferreira 2020 (downloaded) document that no later phonological/prosodic study of Apalaí exists, and web searches (SIL archive, Brazilian repositories, JIPA/phonology journals) found none.

sources.note: The reference-grammar sketch by the same fieldworkers, 15 years after the 12-page 1971 phonemic statement our classification rests on; its suprasegmentals subsection is the fullest published statement of Apalai stress and would settle whether the 'flexibility' and closed-syllable secondary stresses of 1971 were later reanalysed (e.g. as weight-sensitivity). Derbyshire 1999:28 (held) already summarises AP as penultimate, so a change of primary-stress coding is unlikely.
